O1.title: OLED on QWIIC
O1.heading: Turn on the SSD1306 OLED
O1.goal: Connect an SSD1306 OLED to the Pulsar C5 and show a message. This first screen experiment uses only the OLED.
steps: Unplug USB and connect the SSD1306 OLED to QWIIC, or wire only its four pins as shown.
Install Adafruit SSD1306 and Adafruit GFX Library in Arduino IDE.
Open Code to read o1-oled.ino, then upload it. The display shows Pulsar C5 and OLED ready.
O1.note: This example expects a 128 × 64 OLED at I²C address 0x3C. Change the dimensions or address in the code if your module differs. The Pulsar C5 QWIIC connector has no on-board pull-ups; most OLED modules include them.

steps: Unplug USB and connect only the SSD1306 OLED to QWIIC, or wire its four pins as shown.
Open Code, connect the serial REPL and select Install ssd1306.py. This saves the OLED driver on the board.
Run oled.py. The OLED shows Pulsar C5 and MicroPython.
micropython.note: No light sensor is needed. This example expects a 128 × 64 SSD1306 at 0x3C. If you have a 128 × 32 display, set HEIGHT to 32 in oled.py.

03.title: Display
03.heading: The 1.9″ IPS screen
03.goal: Drive the ST7789 display over SPI. Draw each frame in PSRAM, then send it in one go so nothing flickers.
steps: Unplug USB. Wire the 8 display pins as in the table (female-to-male jumpers).
Double-check VCC goes to 3V3, not 5V.
Run the command. You should see red, green and blue bars for 2.5 s.
Then the bench scope: a moving sine wave, uptime and frames per second.
Tell Claude the fps from the monitor and anything that looks off.
03.note: All white or black? Check BLK and RES. Colours inverted? We switch invertDisplay. Garbage? Drop SPI to 20 MHz.

boot.label: Variation 1 · BOOT button
boot.goal: Same wiring as lesson 03. Four scenes show what the S3 can draw: real-time 3D, per-pixel effects, particles and a live dashboard of your chip. The on-board BOOT button switches scenes.
steps: Keep the display wired exactly as in lesson 03. Nothing new to plug in.
Flash with the command above (or tell Claude “go” and it runs it for you).
Watch the 3D torus, then press BOOT to step through Plasma, Fireworks and the Dashboard.
Long-press BOOT (0.6 s) to stop or restart the 12-second auto-cycle.
Open uv run pio device monitor and type scene 2, hud, auto off.
Note fps, draw ms and send ms for each scene and tell Claude. They feed the speed lesson.
boot.note: BOOT only matters at power-on. Don't hold it while pressing RST or plugging in, or the chip waits in flash mode. If that happens, just press RST.

button.label: Variation 2 · Push button
button.goal: The same four scenes, now driven by your own push button on GPIO 5: click, double-click, long press. The screen is an output on 8 wires; the button is an input on 2. This variation shows both together.

0.title: Wiring on the ESP32: screen + button

steps: Unplug USB. Keep the display wired exactly as in lesson 03.
Push the button into the breadboard so it straddles the centre gap, away from the board.

Jumper from leg A to the ESP32's pin 5. On an expansion board that is the socket labelled 5, two past the display's BLK wire on 7. Jumper from the diagonal leg D to any GND. Breadboard holes are not connected to the ESP32, so both wires must end on the ESP32's own sockets.
Plug in and flash with the command above (or tell Claude “go”).
Press the button: click = next scene, double-click = previous, long press = auto-cycle on/off. BOOT does the same.
Open uv run pio device monitor: every click logs how many contact bounces it filtered.
button.note: Never reacts? Check the signal wire really ends on 5, not its neighbour 4, and that both wires end on the ESP32, not on breadboard holes. Always “pressed”? Use diagonally opposite legs.
